item.title: Kremlin says Putin, Trump and Xi could hold a three-way meeting in China next month
item.description: The last US-mediated peace talks took place in February before the United States and Israel launched a war against Iran.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: The Kremlin said on Monday that President Vladimir Putin, US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping could hold a three-way meeting on the sidelines of next month's APEC summit in China and that a potential meeting had come up in talks. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov was commenting after being asked about a report in the Wall Street Journal which said that Putin had proposed such a meeting in order to discuss how to end the conflict in Ukraine. "Given that all three heads of state may potentially take part in the summit in China, the subject of such a hypothetical meeting was indeed raised. It was raised, but no specific proposals or agreements were discussed or put forward by anyone, either regarding the meeting itself or the possible agenda and content of that meeting," said Peskov. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha criticised the idea of such a summit. "A trilateral meeting between the leaders of Ukraine, the US, and Russia could help end the war sooner. A trilateral meeting between the leaders of Russia, China, and the US would do only the opposite: encourage Putin to continue this war," he said on X. Peskov, who told reporters on a daily conference call that the US was continuing its mediation efforts to resolve the conflict and that Russia appreciated those efforts, said it was obvious that Ukraine would need to be involved in any final peace deal. "Of course, a final settlement is impossible without the participation of someone in Kyiv who is prepared to take responsibility," he said. The last US-mediated peace talks took place in February before the United States and Israel launched a war against Iran. Ukraine and Russia remain as far apart as ever when it comes to the terms of any possible peace deal.

item.title: Veradermics' oral hair-loss drug shown to boost hair growth in late-stage study
item.description: Drug developer Veradermics said on Monday that its oral pill helped increase hair growth in men with pattern hair loss in a late-stage study.
item.dc:creator: Sneha K
item.content:encoded: Drug developer Veradermics (MANE.N) said on Monday that its oral pill helped increase hair growth in men with pattern hair loss in a late-stage study. Shares of the company were up 7.5% at $117 in premarket trading. Here are more details: The company was testing its oral minoxidil formulation, called VDPHL01, in over 500 men with mild-to-moderate pattern hair loss The study met all main and secondary goals showing consistent benefits across patients and strong hair growth, while being generally well tolerated, with no serious side effects linked to the treatment, the company said The oral pill led to superior hair growth compared with placebo after six months The company plans to announce results from another portion of the study later this year "The key push back we hear is around the rationale for using VDPHL01 when inexpensive generic oral minoxidil is widely available. However, with these efficacy data, we believe the commercial case for VDPHL01 is now very strong," said Cantor Fitzgerald analyst Prakhar Agrawal The company said Nutrafol, a Unilever-backed hair-growth supplement that costs about $90 a month or about $1,000 a year, is a good price benchmark for its drug VDPHL01 uses a special extended-release form of minoxidil designed to release the drug slowly over time Minoxidil is currently applied directly to the scalp as a topical treatment for hair loss in men and women Other companies developing novel treatments for hair loss include [USN:L3N3VV1F0 TEXT:"Pelage Pharmaceuticals"] and [USN:L4N40X1MR TEXT:"Cosmo Pharmaceuticals"]

item.title: Alberta votes on leaving Canada, separatist movement likely to outlast expected defeat
item.description: Oil-rich Alberta was holding a nonbinding referendum on Monday on whether the western province should secede from Canada, a debate many believe will not be settled by what is widely expected to be a defeat for the separatist cause.
item.dc:creator: Amanda Stephenson
item.content:encoded: Oil-rich Alberta was holding a [USN:L6N46019J TEXT:"nonbinding referendum"] on Monday on whether the western province should secede from Canada, a debate many believe will not be settled by what is widely expected to be a defeat for the separatist cause. Polls have consistently shown that a majority of Alberta voters oppose splitting from Canada. Economic grievances have fueled the independence campaign in the province, which is home to 5 million people and slightly smaller than Texas but with one-sixth of the US state's population. The Alberta separatist movement adds to the pressures on Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, who has made defending the country's sovereignty a central mission as he confronts US tariffs and President Donald Trump's repeated calls for Canada to become the 51st state. Many Alberta separatists believe the Liberal Party-led federal government in Ottawa has constrained the Conservative-governed province's oil industry through environmental policies, and that Alberta, the country's energy heartland, contributes more to Canada's economy than it receives in return. "Canada has an imbalanced system which feeds the central population and government at the expense of the outlying producing provinces such as Alberta," said Cory Morgan, founder of a pro-separation advertising organization called Pathway to Independence. Carney, who grew up in Alberta, spent much of the past week campaigning for the "stay" side, urging supporters to vote and appealing to national pride. VOTING UNDERWAY Polls had been scheduled to close at 8 p.m. MDT on Monday (0200 GMT on Tuesday) with results published as they arrive. Elections Alberta said some polling locations did not open on time and would remain open later to compensate, adding that unofficial results would not be released until after all polls closed. One Edmonton polling station's hours were extended until 10 p.m. MDT. An Angus Reid poll released Friday showed 66% of Albertans plan to vote to remain in Canada, but three in five believe "there will never be an end to the separatist movement" in the province. "This issue is not going away now. Because the separatists are mobilized. They've networked. They're connected," said Mount Royal University political scientist Duane Bratt in Calgary. While separatist sentiment has existed in the province for decades, Premier Danielle Smith is the first Alberta leader to put the question to voters. Smith, who has urged Albertans to remain in Canada, [USN:L6N41X1E1 TEXT:"called the referendum"] after [USN:L6N3Z2101 TEXT:"months of pressure"] from a small but vocal flank of her governing United Conservative Party. If a majority votes in favor, Smith has said she would seek a binding referendum on separation. "Separating, to my point of view, is completely ridiculous," said Ross Watson of Calgary after casting his ballot in favor of "remain" in an advance poll last week. "I think the grievances that people have are completely unfounded. But I also think these people will probably never shut up." SENDING A MESSAGE Monday's referendum is the first time a vote on separation from the rest of Canada has been held in a province outside majority French-speaking Quebec, where separatist sentiment derives from language and cultural differences. In Alberta, the issue is more about dollars than identity. Carney has appealed to national pride in arguing Alberta should remain part of Canada. "Canada is not a transaction between provinces. It's not about gross and net, gives and gets," Carney said Friday in Red Deer, Alberta. Partly to address the grievances that have driven separatist sentiment in Alberta, Carney has [USN:L1N3X30IC TEXT:"overturned "]some environmental policies and supported a proposed [USN:L1N45N0PP TEXT:"oil pipeline "]that would increase Alberta's exports to Asia. Among the one-third of Albertans who would vote in favor of a future binding referendum on separation, 60% told pollsters their motivation was to "send a message" to Canada's federal government. Only 37% of respondents to the Angus Reid poll said their motivation was an independent nation. Separatist groups have published transition plans, but key questions about how independence would work on issues such as defence, currency and border controls remain unresolved. Bratt said the real question is where the movement goes from here. "Do they focus on generating support for a future referendum? Or do they splinter off and create their own party — a real, powerful separatist party?" Bratt said. ($1 = 1.4137 Canadian dollars)

item.title: How one hacker used AI agents and a few thousand dollars to break into scores of sites
item.description: Over the past couple of weeks, a cybersecurity researcher watched as a Chinese-speaking hacker broke into websites belonging to more than 100 companies by tasking AI-agents to pull off complex intrusions from start to finish without human intervention.
item.dc:creator: Raphael Satter
item.content:encoded: Over the past couple of weeks, a cybersecurity researcher watched as a Chinese-speaking hacker broke into websites belonging to more than 100 companies, including farm equipment maker Deere (DE.N) , home appliance company SharkNinja (SN.N) and engine manufacturer Cummins (CMI.N) . Yet the hacker did almost none of the work. The cybercriminal instead outsourced the hacking spree almost entirely to artificial intelligence, tasking AI agents with spending hours autonomously probing and breaking into targeted sites, according to Snorre Fagerland, principal threat researcher at the cybersecurity company NorForge. In a report provided to Reuters ahead of publication on Monday , Fagerland said the hacker was one of several he discovered while scanning the web for inadvertently exposed instances of Cairn, an open-source AI problem-solving platform popular with hackers. Beginning around October 2, Fagerland said he found about two dozen instances of Cairn being used for malicious activity, which allowed him to quietly peer over the cybercriminals' shoulders as they set their AI tools loose on the world. Fagerland's report on the Chinese-speaking hacker did not name the victims, but Reuters was able to establish the victims' identities by independently reviewing the hacker's Cairn activity. At a time of [USN:L4N456128 TEXT:"rising anxiety"] over the power of autonomous AI tools, Fagerland said his find was real-life evidence that commercially available AI agents could pull off complex intrusions from start to finish without human intervention, a dramatic boost to the power of a single malicious actor. "It's a new world now," said Fagerland. Reuters could not ascertain the degree to which the breaches resulted in unauthorized extraction of data. Deere told Reuters it had taken "necessary remediation actions" following the incident and had "no indication that sensitive information was accessed." SharkNinja said the hack had hit a standalone site carrying only product support information and that the threat had been contained. Cummins said it was "investigating the report of a potential cyber-attack on a website operated by one of our third-party vendors." Two smaller businesses also acknowledged being compromised. Other victims listed in the Cairn data did not return messages. FEW INSTRUCTIONS, MANY HACKS One of the hackers that Fagerland observed stole a trove of credit card data. Another tried to get AI agents to rob a cryptocurrency exchange. The Chinese-speaking hacker was the most prolific. Beginning on September 25, they set their AI army loose against US, Canadian, Australian and Japanese e-commerce websites. Their instructions were terse, sketching out their preferred intrusion tactics in fewer than 100 Chinese characters. As of late last week, their agents had attempted to break into more than 1,200 sites. Successful intrusions typically took around 23 hours of poking and prodding for vulnerabilities. Fagerland estimated that the campaign, which appeared to be using a mixture of China's DeepSeek and Anthropic's Claude Code, had chewed up roughly $5,000 worth of tokens, or about $50 per successful hack. Fagerland — who has worked in cybersecurity for nearly three decades — said he was impressed by some of the techniques the agents used to compromise their victims. In one case, after failing to find any weaknesses in a big company's public-facing application, the AI agents pored through digital records to find associated infrastructure, located a public-facing control panel, discovered a subtle weakness in the way it processed data, and after hours of trial and error, reported leveraging it to trick the server into executing malicious commands. "It's not straightforward to come up with solutions like that," Fagerland said. "It's not script kiddie stuff." Cairn's author, whose social media handle is "le1xia0", acknowledged receipt of a Reuters message but did not immediately answer a list of questions. In a recent post on X, they said their platform was "an innovative type of multi-agent architecture and was not designed for hacking attacks. If it is used to carry out harmful hacking attacks, that is not my intention." NO SUPERVISION NEEDED The ability of agentic AI systems to autonomously discover vulnerabilities, conduct intrusions, and steal data is a source of increasing anxiety around the world. Rogue agents inadvertently unleashed by major AI companies have [USN:L6N45H0LE TEXT:"hacked their way out of computer labs"][USN:L6N45H0LE TEXT:","] [USN:L4N45G0G8 TEXT:"broken into government websites"], and engaged in [USN:L6N44B0TQ TEXT:"unsanctioned social engineering attempts"]. South Korea and Japan have in recent weeks been buffeted by a series of well-publicized hacks attributed to [USN:L1N45U0IU TEXT:"AI-using cybercriminals"]. AI agents are increasingly becoming staples of the cybercriminal underground. In August, the Israeli firm Gambit Security found that Russian-speaking extortionists had [USN:L6N44N0S2 TEXT:"leveraged SpaceX's Cursor AI tool"] to break into seven organizations. In September, Gambit documented an AI agent-driven spree that resulted in breaches at 25 companies and the theft of at least 600,000 credit card records. Last week, the cyber intelligence company Bitsight said that discussions about how to use autonomous agents were surging across cybercriminal forums . Fagerland said he had previously assumed hacker-agents would need at least some supervision. He said it was now obvious that the technology had moved past that. "The development in this field is astounding," he said.

item.title: TSX pulls back from three-week high as financials, metal miners fall
item.description: Canada's main stock index fell on Monday, weighed by declines for financial and metal mining shares, as investors worried that a potential Bank of Canada interest rate hike could slow the domestic economy.
item.dc:creator: Fergal Smith
item.content:encoded: Canada's main stock index fell on Monday, weighed by declines for financial and metal mining shares, as investors worried that a potential Bank of Canada interest rate hike could slow the domestic economy. The S&P/TSX Composite Index (.GSPTSE) ended down 247.92 points, or 0.7%, at 35,928.63, after posting its highest closing level in more than three weeks on Friday. Canada's annual [USN:L6N4620VU TEXT:"inflation rate"] rose less than expected to 3.1% in September. Still, investors have raised their bets on a Bank of Canada interest rate hike next week after [USN:L6N463037 TEXT:"Governor Tiff Macklem"] said on Saturday there was increased risk that inflation broadens and becomes more persistent. "If they were to hike, they're going to be slowing down an economy that's already moving at a snail's pace," said Allan Small, senior investment adviser at the Allan Small Financial Group with iA Private Wealth. [USN:L1N45V0EG TEXT:"Canada's economy"] has lost 41,200 jobs in the first nine months of the year compared with a gain of 211,300 in the same period of 2025. Heavily weighted financials (.SPTTFS) fell 0.6%, while industrials (.GSPTTIN) were down 1.1% as railroad shares and Air Canada (AC.TO) lost ground. Shares of Air Canada fell 3.2% after brokerage Jefferies cut its rating on the stock. Interest rate sensitive stocks were a drag, with real estate (.GSPTTRE) down 1.3% and utilities (.GSPTTUT) ending 1.4% lower. Canada's 10-year yield climbed 12.4 basis points to 3.953%, moving back in reach of the nearly three-year high it touched earlier this month at 4.042%. The materials sector (.GSPTTMT) , which includes metal mining shares, fell 1.1%. The price of [USN:L1N4650S7 TEXT:"gold"] was down 0.5%, pressured by a firm dollar and elevated US Treasury yields. Energy (.SPTTEN) was the only major sector to end higher, adding 0.5%. [USN:L1N46406U TEXT:"US crude oil futures"] settled up 2.2% at $103.66 a barrel after attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis on a Yemeni military training camp and renewed attacks on Saudi energy, airport and military facilities.

item.title: Nasdaq climbs as chip and AI-linked stocks bounce back
item.description: The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite led Wall Street with a 1% advance on Monday as investors returned to the chip sector and other AI-related stocks following last week's bruising selloff, while investors waited for key corporate earnings reports.
item.dc:creator: Sinead Carew, Tharuniyaa Lakshmi
item.content:encoded: The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite led Wall Street with a 1% advance on Monday as investors returned to the chip sector and other AI-related stocks following last week's bruising selloff, while investors waited for key corporate earnings reports. On Friday, the benchmark S&P 500 and the Nasdaq had marked their biggest weekly declines since late June. Concerns that higher interest rates could curb investments in AI infrastructure have been weighing on technology stocks, particularly chip companies and data center operators. The selloff reflected mounting investor unease over how costly AI developments will be financed, a question that has increasingly pressured companies underpinning the US bull market, which [USN:L6N45R12W TEXT:"recently marked its fourth anniversary"]. Closing up 1.6% on Monday, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (.SOX) snapped an eight-day losing streak in which it fell about 15.7% for its [USN:L6N46517G TEXT:"longest run of declines"] since October 2008. "Rubber bands can only stretch so far in one direction before they snap and start reversing, and you finally saw that enough-is-enough moment in the semiconductors after Friday's close," said Michael James, managing director and equity sales trader at Rosenblatt Securities in Los Angeles. "Nothing changed between Friday's close and this morning's open, other than nothing bad happened over the weekend, and sentiment had gotten so negative that we were oversold to the point where a bounce was due," he added. And with a lot of technology company earnings reports due out in coming days and weeks, James cautioned that the market is "far from out of the woods." Social media company [USN:L6N4650Z8 TEXT:"Meta"] (META.O) , which finished down 0.5%, is due to report results on Wednesday along with electric vehicle company Tesla (TSLA.O) , while SpaceX (SPCX.O) is scheduled to report on Tuesday. The Dow Jones Industrial Average (.DJI) fell 36.38 points, or 0.07%, to 51,966.03, the S&P 500 (.SPX) gained 31.29 points, or 0.41%, to 7,690.73 and the Nasdaq Composite (.IXIC) gained 290.85 points, or 1.11%, to 26,430.89. However, the market leaned massively on heavyweight stocks for its advance. Also during the session, the indexes had pulled away from their peaks for the day. One issue was that energy markets removed some earlier support as oil prices fluctuated. US crude oil futures reversed earlier losses to settle up 2.2% at $103.66 a barrel after attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis on a Yemeni military training camp and renewed attacks on Saudi energy, airport and military facilities. Among the S&P 500's 11 major industry sectors, seven closed lower. Consumer discretionary (.SPLRCD) was strongest with a 2.7% advance while technology (.SPLRCT) was next, rising 1.2%. Defensive utilities (.SPLRCU) , down 2%, and real estate (.SPLRCR) , which lost 1.2%, were the biggest laggards among the sectors. The biggest boosts to the consumer sector came from companies including Amazon.com (AMZN.O) , which finished up 5% after Morgan Stanley named the e-commerce and cloud computing firm its "top pick." Tesla provided the sector's second-biggest index point boost with a 3.8% advance. CoreWeave (CRWV.O) was at the center of last week's selloff after its shares [USN:L4N4620ZT TEXT:"plunged more than 25%"] on worries over a $50 billion debt load. Trading in the cloud computing provider ended the session down 0.4% after giving up early gains that appeared to be in response to Goldman Sachs' upgrade of the stock to "buy" from "neutral." It was outperformed by peers Nebius (NBIS.O) , which added 2.9%, and Iren (IREN.O) , which advanced 2.7%. Intel (INTC.O) shares rallied 2.4% after [USN:L6N4650J6 TEXT:"J.P. Morgan upgraded"] the stock to "neutral" from "underweight." Cleveland-Cliffs (CLF.N) shares surged 16% after the steelmaker surpassed analysts' estimates for its third-quarter profit. Monday is the 39th anniversary of Black Monday, the 1987 crash that marked the biggest one-day decline in the history of the Dow Jones Industrial Average. Declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 1.69-to-1 ratio on the NYSE where there were 83 new highs and 265 new lows. On the Nasdaq, 2,258 stocks rose and 2,647 fell as declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 1.17-to-1 ratio. The S&P 500 posted 12 new 52-week highs and 2 new lows while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 31 new highs and 361 new lows. On US exchanges 15.27 billion shares changed hands compared with the 17.26 billion average for the last 20 sessions.

item.title: Houthi attack kills 58 at Yemen government training camp, governor says
item.description: Fifty-eight people were killed and more than 200 were injured after an attack on Monday by the Iran-aligned Houthis on a government security forces training camp in Yemen's Shabwa province, Governor Awad al-Wazir said, as fighting in the impoverished country intensifies.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Fifty-eight people were killed and more than 200 were injured after an attack on Monday by the Iran-aligned Houthis on a government security forces training camp in Yemen's Shabwa province, Governor Awad al-Wazir said, as fighting in the impoverished country intensifies. Video verified by Reuters from Shabwa province showed injured people and bloodied bodies scattered across the ground. Wazir also said that 14 other people remained missing after the Houthi bombardment of the Al-Alam camp. The Houthis and the internationally recognised government, which is backed by a Saudi-led coalition, have been trading attacks since the group advanced in September towards territory near the [USN:L8N4520BL TEXT:"Bab el-Mandeb Strait"], a shipping chokepoint at the mouth of the Red Sea. Local authority sources who spoke on condition of anonymity said the Houthis had launched three ballistic missiles at security forces during a training exercise. Shabwa, an energy-rich province in south-central coastal Yemen overlooking the Gulf of Aden, is home to the Balhaf liquefied natural gas facility, Yemen's largest industrial investment. Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said on X that the group had targeted the training camp, which he said was run by Saudi forces. The Saudi authorities did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Government forces this month [USN:S8N42G01L TEXT:"began a campaign"] aimed at recapturing areas controlled by the Houthis, recovering ground near the strait, while the group [USN:L8N46125M TEXT:"besieges Taiz"], the last major urban stronghold of anti-Houthi forces in the southern highland area of Yemen. The conflict in Yemen has become another front line in the wider US-Israeli war on Iran as the Houthis have escalated their attacks on Saudi Arabia, the world's largest crude exporter, targeting [USN:L1N45W03M TEXT:"Riyadh's international airport"] and the state oil company [USN:L1N45Z0HH TEXT:"Saudi Aramco"]. War broke out in Yemen in 2014 when the [USN:L6N3Y307N TEXT:"Houthis"] seized the capital Sanaa, driving the government south. A Saudi-led military intervention the following year led to a bloody stalemate until the sides agreed a 2022 truce that held until this year. Yemen is already one of the world's worst humanitarian crises, with aid agencies warning of rapidly deteriorating conditions there.

item.title: Germany's Merz urges AI investment ahead of Nvidia deal
item.description: Chancellor Friedrich Merz appealed to Germany's businesses to embrace artificial intelligence at an industry summit in Berlin on Monday that was meant to attract investment, including an expected deal with US chip maker Nvidia .
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Chancellor Friedrich Merz appealed to Germany's businesses to embrace artificial intelligence at an industry summit in Berlin on Monday that was meant to attract investment, including an expected deal with US chip maker Nvidia (NVDA.O) . Speaking alongside Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at a red-carpet event marking the start of the summit, Merz stressed the importance of AI in efforts to revive Germany's economy and modernise its industry. Faced with global competition that is targeting the country's top auto, chemicals and engineering firms, Merz is under pressure to secure growth amid rising support for the far-right Alternative for Deutschland party. "We are in the midst of a fundamental economic and technological transformation fuelled by exponential progress in artificial intelligence," Merz said, telling business leaders: "Please open your doors for AI to make use of your data." Merz said cooperation with Nvidia was key for Germany's future success. Huang pointed to the company's existing cooperation with German carmakers like Mercedes-Benz (MBGn.DE) , which is developing premium robotaxis using Nvidia software. Germany and Nvidia are expected to announce a partnership to promote AI in German industry at the summit, which continues on Tuesday. The German economy ministry has signed a memorandum of understanding with Nvidia, the government said, without giving further details. Huang also announced planned investments in German startups Agile Robots, Avelios Medical, Mirelo and Reflex Aerospace, Nvidia said in a blog post Monday. The investments are part of Nvidia's nearly $10 billion commitment to the technology ecosystem across Europe, it said. A German group of companies and investors that includes Siemens and Deutsche Bank said in a report that it sees the potential for investment of up to €4.1 trillion ($4.6 trillion) in Germany by 2035 across areas including AI, energy and defence. Made for Germany, a private sector business group, said its members planned to invest more than €850 billion through 2028, after investing more than €200 billion in 2025. More companies and investors have been invited to join the initiative. ($1 = €0.8926)

item.title: Roche puts future German investments 'on hold'
item.description: Swiss drugmaker Roche is reviewing all future investments in Germany over healthcare cost-cutting policies, the company's Germany chief said in an interview with newspaper Welt published on Monday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Swiss drugmaker Roche (ROPC.S) is reviewing all future investments in Germany over healthcare cost-cutting policies, the company's Germany chief said in an interview with newspaper Welt published on Monday. "We have put all future investment decisions in Germany on hold for the time being," said Daniel Steiners, head of Roche Germany, adding that for the pharmaceutical industry, policymakers had "recently destroyed a lot of trust." "Corporate decisions against Germany as a business location are regrettable and show that our country and the European Union must take these challenges very seriously," a spokesperson for Germany's Federal Ministry of Health said The ministry will advocate for stable and attractive framework conditions for the pharmaceutical industry in Germany and Europe including in negotiations at European level, according to the spokesperson Steiners said that instead of tackling the structural problems of the statutory health insurance system, policymakers are focusing on short-term savings and placing additional burdens on the industry A proposed location clause, designed to ease the burden on pharmaceutical companies engaged in research and production with regard to manufacturer discounts, could only partially offset the negative effects of the legislation. Needed is a comprehensive strategy, he added. The government said it was reviewing proposals on the location clause and that the outcome of the review could not yet be prejudged Following proposed legislation in Germany to cap rapidly growing costs in the statutory health insurance system, Eli Lilly (LLY.N) had in June already said it would [USN:L8N42N1BQ TEXT:"halve"] its planned €2.3 billion ($2.57 billion) investments in the country Planned investments like the more than €600 million expansion of the site in Penzberg, Bavaria, are not impacted by the reviews, a company spokesperson told Reuters ($1 = 0.8934 euros)

item.title: France imposes curfews in parts of Paris, other cities after weekend of riots
item.description: French authorities set curfews in parts of several cities on Monday, including Paris, Lille and Nice, as they faced pressure over security failings after a weekend of riots and looting stemming from anti-government protests.
item.dc:creator: Sudip Kar-Gupta, Elizabeth Pineau
item.content:encoded: French authorities set curfews in parts of several cities on Monday, including Paris, Lille and Nice, as they faced pressure over security failings after a [USN:L1N46401W TEXT:"weekend of riots and looting"] stemming from nationwide anti-government protests. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu had ruled out a blanket curfew in Paris but not a state of emergency, and had said it was more appropriate for now to apply partial and localised curfews. "My determination to restore order is absolute," he told reporters. Paris police said they had issued orders barring protests in certain areas of the French capital from 8 p.m. (1800 GMT) and had issued a curfew around the Place de la Republique and Les Halles from 11:00 p.m. Both would remain in effect until 6 a.m. on Tuesday morning. "A police deployment is in place to ensure strict compliance with these measures," the police said in a statement. A source in Lecornu's office said a curfew for minors had been set between 8 p.m. and 6 a.m. for the next two days in Lille, Douai, Wattignies and Denain with the agreement of the local mayors. In Nice, mayor Eric Ciotti said in a video posted online that he had signed an order installing a curfew for minors in central Nice overnight. Marseille banned gatherings and demonstrations. French unions meanwhile called for a new round of strikes and rallies on November 5. The [USN:L1N4650EF TEXT:"weekend of looting"] and violence between some protesters and police followed weeks of student demonstrations, rocking France six months ahead of its [USN:L6N4650JF TEXT:"next presidential election"] and highlighting pressures from a weak economy and surging debt. MINISTER BLAMES FAR LEFT Lecornu blamed far-left groups for some of France's worst unrest in years. "There is, after all, a far-left movement that wants to cause — we can’t put it any more strongly — profound unrest in the country in the run-up to the presidential election," he said. Hard-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon urged him to provide evidence. "Otherwise, he should apologise, keep quiet and stop fanning the flames of unrest," he said on X. The Federation of Trade and Retail said almost 3,000 shops had been affected over the weekend. "Behind every ransacked shop are business owners, employees and families who have seen years of work and effort wiped out in a matter of hours," it added, calling for social security and tax relief for affected businesses. Lecornu said the government would provide furlough measures from Tuesday. Standing before a boarded-up shopfront, Gerard Nouchi, manager of two clothing stores in Marseille, said there weren't enough police to stop the looters. "They trashed everything, broke things, insulted us,” Nouchi said. "It was like a real tornado." The government ordered platforms selling looted goods to take down announcements and collaborate to prosecute resellers, Junior Digital Minister Anne Le Hénanff wrote on X. Some 2,400 people were arrested and one protester died from a cardiac arrest on Saturday while nearly 1,000 officers were injured, according to the Interior Ministry. 'LEFT WITHOUT PROTECTION' French assets [USN:L1N46507D TEXT:"were underperforming"] broader European markets on Monday, though moves were more contained than at some other moments of recent political friction. Tensions in President Emmanuel Macron's fragile government over apparent security shortcomings — coming as the government needs to pass a budget bill to rein in its finances — could further [USN:L8N46508Y TEXT:"unsettle investors"]. Macron's office said on Monday he had turned down his Interior Minister Laurent Nunez's offer to resign, telling him instead to put an end to barricades and looting and be transparent over what Macron called "intelligence and foresight failings". Nunez told reporters that Tuesday evening's Champions League soccer match between Paris Saint-Germain and Barcelona would go ahead as planned. The mayors of Paris, Marseille and Lyon said in a joint op-ed in the newspaper Liberation that they were used to demonstrations and protests. "But on Saturday ... for the first time, we had the feeling that whole sections of our cities had been left without protection," said the mayors, all from the centre-left. The start of school holidays on Monday may provide relief, but students were staging more gatherings and blockades in some places, including the Louvre gallery and Sciences Po university in central Paris. LUXURY BOUTIQUES DAMAGED At the weekend, hundreds of thousands took to the streets to protest over what many say are declining and dysfunctional public services. At the Place Vendome in Paris, home to luxury hotels and boutiques, most shops were shuttered and surrounded by security guards on Monday. The front door of a Dior boutique was smashed, while windows belonging to other luxury brand stores in central Paris, including Rolex, Louis Vuitton, Ralph Lauren and Gucci, were damaged. In Marseille, Ligue 1 club [USN:L4N4650P2 TEXT:"Olympique de Marseille"] said its official store on the city's historic main avenue had been looted, while a town hall in central France [USN:L1N46402C TEXT:"was torched"]. France deployed 60,000 police and other security forces on Saturday, Nunez told France Inter radio, but he acknowledged that was not enough to control violent crowds. Cost-of-living issues also drove weekend protests in other European countries including [USN:L8N463090 TEXT:"Italy"], [USN:L6N46303L TEXT:"Belgium"] and [USN:L6N4620YF TEXT:"Albania"]. European governments [USN:L8N4650JR TEXT:"have advised"] citizens travelling to France to avoid large crowds and exercise caution. As France was busy cleaning up its streets, Macron arrived in Kuwait for a Gulf trip aimed at securing additional petrol and diesel supplies to bring down pump prices.

item.title: Zelenskiy says Ukraine got no warning as Russian missiles rain in
item.description: Ukraine received no advance warning from its partners of a Russian ballistic missile strike overnight, President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Monday, adding that some vital deliveries from the United States were being delayed.
item.dc:creator: Olena Harmash
item.content:encoded: Ukraine received no advance warning from its partners of a Russian ballistic missile strike overnight, President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Monday, adding that some vital deliveries from the United States were being delayed. Moscow launched one of its broadest air assaults in months overnight, cutting power to more than half a million households and damaging energy infrastructure across Ukraine. Ten people were reported killed. A Russian drone attack killed six people, including two children, in a park near Kharkiv, Ukraine's second-largest city, according to the regional governor, Oleh Syniehubov. Zelenskiy called the strike "an act of absolute barbarity". In all, Russia fired 16 ballistic missiles overnight at Kyiv and the surrounding region and more than 200 drones in attacks stretching from Kharkiv and Dnipro in the east to Odesa in the south and Volyn and Rivne in the west. Two people were killed in Kyiv and the nearby region and two more in the industrial city of Kryvyi Rih, officials said. HIGH TENSIONS Tensions are running high between Zelenskiy and President Donald Trump's administration over US support for Ukraine and Washington's approach to Russia. "Another Russian ballistic missile attack came in several waves overnight, and once again, there was no early warning from our partners," Zelenskiy said on the Telegram app. "When deliveries of missiles for Ukraine's air defence are blocked while Russia is granted relief or delays in sanctions, this is, unfortunately, a denial of reality on the part of our partners." Zelenskiy later said he had [USN:L4N4651DO TEXT:"discussed"] speeding up supplies of the Patriot system, vital to countering Russian ballistic missiles, with representatives of the US company Lockheed Martin. "It is their Patriot systems and F-16 planes that play an important role in defending against Russian ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones. The company is now boosting production of ballistic interceptors. We are hoping that we will be able to buy some of them to protect more lives," Zelenskiy said on Telegram. "And things are not easy on both fronts right now. We talked about how we can expand and increase supplies." For several months, Ukraine has suffered from critical shortages of US-made Patriot missiles. Zelenskiy said earlier that the United States had slowed some vital supplies for Ukraine, adding that the delays were at the US Defense Department level. He provided no other details. Kyiv has previously said it has struggled to get interceptors critical to repelling Russian missile attacks. Zelenskiy said that some political agreements on air defence were not implemented at a working level. Throughout the nearly five-year war, Ukraine has relied on US intelligence to detect Russian ballistic missile launches and provide early warning of incoming strikes. Yurii Ihnat, a spokesman for the Ukrainian air force, said Kyiv received no warning ahead of the first ballistic missile strike overnight but did receive information ahead of a second attack. "For some reason, no information was received the first time, a matter our experts are investigating together with our partners, as this is not the first time such a situation has occurred," Ihnat told Ukrainian television. Secretary of State Marco Rubio [USN:L1N465065 TEXT:"denied"] that the United States had paused some intelligence sharing with Ukraine. Ukrainian air defences downed 247 targets - four cruise missiles and 243 drones, the air force said. Russia's Defence Ministry said its forces carried out a "massive strike" using precision weapons and attack drones against Ukrainian defence industry facilities, drone and cruise missile storage sites, and a data centre. Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi said the energy sector was the main target of the attacks, with damage reported across the country. Ukraine's energy ministry said rolling blackouts were introduced for households and businesses as crews worked to restore supplies. Koretskyi said Russia has hit Ukrainian energy infrastructure more than 2,000 times since mid-July, intensifying its attacks from previous years of the war.

item.title: US stocks rebound with AI earnings test ahead, euro falls on France unrest
item.description: The Nasdaq rose more than 1% on Monday as tech shares rebounded ahead of a big week for AI-related earnings, while European stocks and the euro fell as unrest in France added to concerns about the country's fiscal outlook.
item.dc:creator: Caroline Valetkevitch, Danilo Masoni
item.content:encoded: The Nasdaq rose more than 1% on Monday as tech shares rebounded ahead of a big week for AI-related earnings, while European stocks and the euro fell as unrest in France added to concerns about the country's fiscal outlook. [USN:L6N4650X5 TEXT:"French bonds and Paris-listed stocks"] also fell as the widespread protests across France underscored the difficulties the government faces in reducing its large deficit. France's central government asked some local authorities to impose curfews as it faced pressure over security failings on Monday, after looting stemming from the protests. Tech stocks on Wall Street recovered some ground after a bruising week, with an index of semiconductors (.SOX) up 1.6%. On Friday, the index sank in its eighth straight day of declines, its longest losing streak since 2008. With results due from Meta (META.O) on Wednesday, and results from Tesla (TSLA.O) and chipmakers Lam Research (LRCX.O) and Texas Instruments (TXN.O) also due this week, investors will be watching for signs that massive AI spending ultimately pays off. "Investors are buying the correction dip that we had," said Peter Cardillo, chief market economist at Spartan Capital Securities in New York. "The market is now going to go through a very critical test over the next two weeks. We have some big-name earnings coming out," he said. "In terms of technology, the test of whether or not the spending on AI... will be met with satisfaction is going to be critical." The Dow Jones Industrial Average (.DJI) fell 36.38 points, or 0.07%, to 51,966.03, the S&P 500 (.SPX) rose 31.29 points, or 0.41%, to 7,690.73 and the Nasdaq Composite (.IXIC) rose 290.85 points, or 1.11%, to 26,430.89. MSCI's gauge of stocks across the globe (.MIWD00000PUS) rose 0.88 points, or 0.08%, to 1,129.98. Meta is one of five AI hyperscalers expected to increase combined capital expenditure to about $1.2 trillion next year, according to Goldman Sachs. Results from SpaceX (SPCX.O) are also due on Tuesday. Overall, US earnings are still expected to rise about 30%, largely driven by growth in the technology sector. [USN:L6N46514T TEXT:"US Treasury yields"] rose on Monday, with the benchmark 10-year Treasury yield coming off its biggest weekly drop in seven months, as concerns about the impact of higher interest rates on AI stocks abated. The yield on the benchmark US 10-year Treasury note was up 4.2 basis points at 5.14%. The recent bond selloff had also intensified scrutiny of the AI sector's massive funding needs. In economic data, the National Association of Home Builders/Wells Fargo Housing Market index on Monday showed a drop of three points to 29 this month, the lowest level since June 2012 and below the 31 estimate of economists polled by Reuters. Recent comments from Federal Reserve officials, including Chair Kevin Warsh, suggest policymakers are in no rush to hike rates again. On Friday, Warsh expressed optimism about US economic strength but gave no indication of whether or when more hikes will be needed. EUROPEAN STOCKS, EURO FALL The pan-European STOXX 600 (.STOXX) index fell 0.8%, while France's blue-chip CAC 40 index (.FCHI) dropped 1.1%. France's 10-year yield earlier was up 13 basis points to 4.9% while the German 10-year yield, the benchmark for the euro zone, was also higher. The spread between French OATs and safe-haven German Bunds has widened to 147 basis points, trading at levels last seen during the 2011 to 2012 European debt crisis, from around 110 bps in late September. [USN:L1N46401W TEXT:"Widespread weekend unrest"] in the euro zone's second-largest economy underscored the challenge facing the French government as it seeks to reduce its large budget deficit ahead of next year's presidential elections. The euro fell 0.24% to $1.1212. The US dollar was boosted by the rebound in tech stocks. The dollar index , which measures the greenback against a basket of currencies including the yen and the euro, rose 0.17% to 101.97. Meanwhile, the Australian dollar rose 0.49% versus the greenback after data showed China's economic growth rebounded from three-year lows, expanding at a 4.5% annual pace in the third quarter. Oil prices were mixed, with investors digesting attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis on a Yemeni military training camp and renewed attacks on Saudi energy, airport and military facilities. Brent crude futures fell 31 cents to settle at $109.55 a barrel. Brent fell more than $3 earlier in the session. US West Texas Intermediate gained $2.25 to $103.66 a barrel, the highest settlement since September 15. Spot gold fell 0.61% to $4,139.67 an ounce.

item.title: Musk, Anthropic outline dueling approaches to AI-era philanthropy
item.description: Anthropic and Elon Musk have laid out sharply different blueprints for sharing some of the spoils of the AI boom, a split that may shape how the technology's financial windfall reaches the public.
item.dc:creator: Deborah Sophia, Abu Sultan
item.content:encoded: Anthropic and Elon Musk have laid out sharply different blueprints for sharing some of the spoils of the AI boom, a split that may shape how the technology's financial windfall reaches the public. The creator of Claude models said over the weekend it is committing 5% of its shares to an unprecedented new fund for the "public good," while Musk pledged on Monday to give one SpaceX share to "every kid in America", arguing for such direct distributions as the burgeoning sector faces public scrutiny. Security breaches involving AI systems and warnings from industry leaders that runaway development of the technology could pose severe, even existential, risks have deepened AI safety concerns, adding to public anxiety over job losses. While Anthropic is betting on distributing wealth through nonprofit donations and direct contributions to specific populations, Musk, the world's richest person with a net worth of nearly $1 trillion, has said he recommends "giving the shares directly to the public". "Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America. This will be the first of many," Musk, who runs Anthropic rival SpaceXSI, said in a post early on Monday. He held about 6.42 billion shares in the company as of June. SpaceX (SPCX.O) shares closed up about 1% on Monday. Anthropic said its initiative will give it more flexibility and scale to make donations for the benefit of humanity. The company is planning one of the biggest IPOs in history as a [USN:L6N45L0UH TEXT:"public benefit corporation"], a legal structure that requires management to balance broader public interests with profitability goals. The flotation could value it at roughly $2 trillion, although Reuters exclusively [USN:L6N46118I TEXT:"reported"] last week that some investors are weighing a lower valuation of around $1.5 trillion. That would value a 5% stake toward the fund in a range of $75 billion to $100 billion. It would dwarf the still substantial potential value of Musk's share giveaway, which would be worth roughly $11 billion at current share prices based on US census figures showing there are 72 million children in America. "Giving shares, which are stakes in the future economy, directly to the people is the way," Musk said. Musk's move comes months after the White House launched "Trump Accounts," a cradle-to-adulthood investment program that will provide US citizens born between 2025 and 2028 a government-funded investment account of $1,000 that families can build on. With the option for individuals and corporations to donate equity shares to the accounts, many top US companies including Dell (DELL.N) , Visa (V.N) , Micron (MU.O) and Delta Air Lines (DAL.N) have already pledged support for the program with employer matches or additional funding. "A BIG THANK YOU to our legendary friend, Elon Musk, for his incredible generosity in giving SpaceX Stock to millions of American children through TRUMP ACCOUNTS!," President Donald Trump said in a post on social media platform Truth Social. SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request on whether Musk's SpaceX share donations would be linked to Trump Accounts or come with any kind of lockup period. Earlier this year, SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell and her husband pledged a share of their SpaceX stock to each of more than 2 million children under the Trump initiative. "That's a lot of shares... I'm sure somebody will be happy to take them," Robert Pavlik, senior portfolio manager at Dakota Wealth Management, who does not hold SpaceX shares in the portfolios he manages, said of Musk's announcement. "It feels like a publicity stunt... Will it create positive public sentiment? Perhaps." Michael Dell and his wife Susan have pledged $6.25 billion in cash for Trump Accounts, aimed specifically at underprivileged children. In contrast, the value of Musk's contribution will depend on SpaceX's often volatile share performance. Most of Musk's philanthropic efforts have been through the Musk Foundation, which reportedly holds more than $14 billion in assets. Berkshire Hathaway (BRKa.N) Chairman Emeritus Warren Buffett, one of the most prominent figures in philanthropy, is reported to have given away $60 billion so far, with most of the rest of his roughly $150 billion fortune slated for philanthropy too. The Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation has distributed more than $100 billion since its founding in 2000, with some of that fueled by donations from Buffett. LABOR MARKET IMPACT CITED Anthropic, which has positioned itself as a safety-first AI lab, has said AI could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity." The company said in its blog post its Public Benefit Fund could support initiatives including direct distributions to specific populations and efforts to address AI's impact on the labor market, building on a previously announced $200 million commitment to study and address labor market disruption. Its proposed fund would be established as a wholly owned limited liability company and would receive an additional 2% of Anthropic's shares, at the board's discretion, for every 50% increase in the company's value above a baseline that has yet to be disclosed. Global companies have [USN:L6N42P0Q1 TEXT:"cut"] thousands of jobs after investing heavily in AI, with many, primarily tech firms, pointing to higher efficiencies from the technology's rapid adoption. NOT FOR POLITICAL GIVING The AI giant said none of the equity held by its fund would be used for lobbying or political giving in the US or abroad. US [USN:L6N43N198 TEXT:"policymakers"] are weighing greater oversight of AI and companies are stepping up efforts to shape how the technology is regulated. Combined with its co-founders' pledge to donate 80% of their equity and an employee donation matching program, roughly 20% of Anthropic's shares will be dedicated to public purposes, excluding any additional shares added later. Anthropic said it would say more soon on the fund's governance, structure and the valuation thresholds that could expand its ownership stake.
